newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Strong June Hungary output figures point to growth.
newsitem.headline: Strong June Hungary output figures point to growth.

text.p: Better-than-expected industrial output figures for June offer evidence that high foreign direct investment is helping Hungary in its push towards sustainable growth, analysts said on Wednesday.
"The monthly increase is more than encouraging," said Csaba Varga of Citibank. "These figures are even better than expected."
According to figures published on Wednesday by Hungary's Central Statistical Office (KSH) industrial output rose 5.4 percent in June and 16.9 percent in the year up to June.
This compares to a 1.6 percent monthly fall in May and a yearly rise of only 1.7 percent.
The KSH added that industrial output in the first six months of this year was 7.8 percent up from the same period of 1996.
A recent Reuters poll of analysts put the expected first half increase over January to June 1996 at between five and seven percent.
Varga said the figures showed that Hungary was benefiting from high levels of foreign direct investment and that exporters were successfully maintaining their share of Western markets.
"The major part of industrial output comes from export-oriented companies and if you look at the breakdown for export markets, 70 percent go to OECD countries," he said.

David Mars of SBC Warburg in London said the figures have to be viewed in the context of a worldwide phenomenon of good June data, which had one extra working day compared to last year while May had one less.
"Hungary joined the club of many countries with good June output figures -- if you take May and June together you get closer to the true picture," he said.
"The picture is still that Hungary is recovering from the 1995 crisis and it is well on its way to five percent growth next year."

Mars said foreign direct investment in Hungary which, according to trade ministry figures accounts for up to 35 percent of all investment in Central and Eastern Europe since 1990, is beginning to show itself in output and trade figures as greenfield investments reach maturity.
"Now you see the goods being produced," he said. "Western Europe is well into the middle of a strong economic recovery, most of Hungary's exports go there.
"It has a strong competitive position on costs and the quality of its labour and as a location for production."
Varga sees production and export-led growth continuing, with GDP reaching three percent this year, compared to government forecasts of 2.5 percent.
"I don't see any factors that will endanger the general good-looking trend," he said.
